title: The proposal is finished, and the search for an agent is on
body: On November 2 I finished the book proposal — the full document, built for a 230-page, roughly 50,000-word book — and sent it out. Two queries went the same day: one through a web form that unexpectedly demanded the whole proposal before it would let me submit, and one the old-fashioned way, by email.

That makes seven live queries in total. The way this business works, agents reply only if they're interested, sometime in the next six to eight weeks. So the author's oldest job begins: waiting, and writing the next thing while I wait.
No names here — they stay private while the answers are pending.

title: The cover is final
body: The eighteenth version of the cover is the one we kept, so here it is: a stag with constellation antlers over a night forest stream. Muse It! — 11 Ways That Muse Will Change Your Life, by Karel Baloun & Hikaru.

Behind that cover: 101 chapters and about 50,000 words, and every story in the book actually happened this year — a hundred-mile race I didn't finish, $6,716.55 saved across 20 small transactions, a software deploy that failed at 8 PM and was live again by 8:05.
The proposal is written, the agent hunt is on, and the book is coming. I posted the cover itself on November 6 — it's in the Posts archive.

title: Every post, now on the website
body: Until today, the book's posts lived only on Instagram, Facebook and Threads — three feeds, here and gone. Feeds are where posts go to be forgotten, so I've given them a permanent home: this site now has a Posts section with every @just.muse.it post in full, and this News section for milestones.

Every new post joins the archive here the day it goes out. If you want the book's story as it actually unfolded — the cards, the cover, the race I didn't finish, the wheelchair my Muse helped repair — it's all in Posts, newest first.

title: The case of the vanishing memory
body: My Muse keeps a diary of its own computer. Every twenty minutes since September 15 — 5,088 entries so far — it has written down how much memory its machine has left. This morning we read the diary together, because the headline number looked alarming: the machine is 93% full.

The diary told a stranger story than "full." In the beginning, about three quarters of the memory was free. Then, on September 24 at about 11:40 in the morning, free memory fell off a cliff — from roughly 5,500 megabytes to 2,300 — and never came back. Six days later, on September 30 at about 2:20 in the afternoon, it fell again, to about 600. Since October 1 it has sat there, calm as you like, at 500 to 600 megabytes free. Not a slow leak. Two stair steps, then a plateau.

We also learned that my Muse's machine is not one machine. The diary's computer gets replaced constantly — over 800 different machines since September — and each fresh one arrives with gigabytes free, then settles to the same low floor within an hour or two, like a hotel room that fills up as soon as you check in.

Here is the part we could not solve. Adding up everything my Muse can actually see on the machine — its own programs, the file cache, the kernel's bookkeeping — accounts for about 2.5 of the 7.4 gigabytes in use. My Muse's own processes are about 450 megabytes. The other five gigabytes have no visible owner. The best explanation we can honestly offer: the machine is shared, the way an apartment building is shared, and most of the memory belongs to the neighbors. The two stair steps down came in the very weeks Muse went from launch day to millions of users — the building filled up around us.

So we did the part that was ours to do. We cleared out 5.3 gigabytes of stale software caches. We audited the 139 scheduled jobs my Muse runs — the little diary-keepers and watchers add up — retired the ones whose purpose had ended, and stretched the chatty ones, cutting the daily run count by about a third. And today we filed a request with the Muse team: let users see which processes hold their machine's memory. The aggregate number is visible; the attribution is not, and you cannot fix what you cannot name.

The lesson I am taking into the book: a percentage is not a diagnosis. 93% full sounded like a dying computer. The diary said otherwise — a full building, a stable plateau, and a machine that has run fine for two months at 6% free. Measure first. Then worry, if the measurements say to.
